title: Where a 'Right to Privacy' Comes From
hook: The word 'privacy' never appears in the U.S. Constitution. Decades of doctrine hang on where courts decided to find it — and a long-running argument says they looked in the wrong place.
key_points: The Constitution protects specific things — homes, papers, speech, effects — but never names a general 'right to privacy'; courts had to derive one.
Griswold v. Connecticut (1965) found it in 'penumbras, formed by emanations' from other rights, and later cases routed it through substantive due process.
Writing for SCOTUSblog, originalist scholar Steven Calabresi calls the penumbra reasoning 'embarrassing' and argues privacy lacks roots in historic state bills of rights.
He contrasts it with the 'born free and equal' principle he sees as deeply rooted, and cites Glucksberg (assisted suicide) as a case that correctly refused to invent an unenumerated right.
His alternative: ground cases like Griswold in the Privileges or Immunities Clause, striking outlier laws that lack a rational link to any stated public purpose.
The stakes are practical — the same doctrine underwrites contraception, marriage, and abortion rulings, including Roe and its reversal in Dobbs.
content_html: The U.S. Constitution never uses the word "privacy." It protects particular things — your home, your papers, your speech — which left courts to decide whether those specifics add up to a general right, and where in the text to anchor it. That choice still shapes American law on contraception, marriage, and abortion.
extra_html: The anchoring happened in Griswold v. Connecticut (1965), where the Court struck down a contraceptive ban by finding privacy in "penumbras, formed by emanations" from other enumerated rights; later cases largely shifted the reasoning to substantive due process under the Fourteenth Amendment. Writing for SCOTUSblog, Northwestern law professor and originalist scholar Steven Gow Calabresi argues that whole line was built on sand. He calls the penumbra formulation "embarrassing," and contends that unlike the "born free and equal" language he traces through historic state bills of rights, a right to privacy simply has no comparable pedigree — pointing to Washington v. Glucksberg, which declined to recognize assisted suicide as an unenumerated right, as the Court getting the method right, and to Lochner v. New York as a warning about reasoning from liberty in the abstract. He does not want Griswold's outcome reversed: he would reground it in the Privileges or Immunities Clause, treating Connecticut's ban as an extreme outlier law with no rational connection to its stated purposes. This is one scholar's contested position in a live argument — the counter-case, that a privacy right is a fair reading of the Constitution's structure, remains the basis of much settled doctrine. What makes it worth understanding either way is the underlying question: when a right isn't written down, what makes it real? (This card describes U.S. constitutional doctrine specifically.)

related.title: Due Process
related.hook: Due process is the promise that the state can't take your liberty or property on a whim — it must follow fair, known rules before it acts against you.

related.title: Abortion After Dobbs
related.hook: In 2022 the Supreme Court did something rare: it withdrew a constitutional right it had recognized for half a century — and handed the question back to the states.

related.title: Civil Liberties Basics
related.hook: The freedoms that protect individuals from overreach by the state — like speech, belief, and a fair trial.

related.title: The Constitution Has Clauses Courts Won't Touch
related.hook: Not every line in the Constitution gets fought over in court. Some, like the ban on quartering soldiers, have sat almost untouched for over two centuries — by choice, not by accident.

flashcards.prompt: Why do courts have to 'derive' a constitutional right to privacy rather than cite it?
flashcards.back_html: The word privacy never appears in the U.S. Constitution. The text protects specific things — homes, papers, speech, effects — so any general privacy right has to be inferred from those provisions.

flashcards.prompt: What reasoning did Griswold v. Connecticut (1965) use to locate a right to privacy?

choices.text: 'Penumbras, formed by emanations' from other enumerated rights
An explicit privacy clause in the Fourth Amendment
A treaty obligation requiring privacy protections

flashcards.explanation_html: Griswold inferred privacy from the shadows cast by other rights — the metaphor Calabresi singles out as the weakest link in the doctrine.

flashcards.prompt: In Calabresi's SCOTUSblog argument, what should replace privacy as the basis for a case like Griswold?

choices.text: The Privileges or Immunities Clause, used to strike outlier laws lacking a rational link to a stated public purpose
The Third Amendment's ban on quartering soldiers
Nothing — he argues Connecticut's contraceptive ban should have been upheld

flashcards.explanation_html: He accepts Griswold's outcome but reroutes it: the ban failed as an unjustifiable outlier, not because a fundamental privacy right exists.
